utterances.text: Your Honour, considering again the Prosecution's perspective on this is that Mr. Andan did confirm some of the details in the Bosnian statement, that Mr. Zulic was arrested, that Mladic was there, those sorts of things, and that he has sufficiently provided enough information to -- to allow the document to come in as authentic. We believe he doesn't have reason to doubt that Mr. Zulic reported the document or that reported the information in the document. In terms of evaluating his statement, Mr. Andan's statement, we suggest that it's in the interest of fairness and in the interest of justice in trying to assess his testimony that it would be appropriate to consider as well the statements of Mr. Zulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any case law in support of your position in that if once the statement is taken at the time by the local authorities, that his statement taken later with the specific purposes to use it in the ICTY proceedings, that that is not subject any further to the formalities of 92 bis and 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, off the top of my head I do not -- what I would ask is that we MFI these documents and that I could provide supplementary material with respect to admission at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, for the first one that may be different but let me -- Mr. Stojanovic, what would be your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, like last time, we are opposed to having this statement admitted into evidence. The statement of a person and this was not done for the needs of this court and it's not a proper 92 bis or 92 ter statement. We had an identical situation last week and, again, we were opposed to having such statements admitted into evidence, especially after the witness spoke today and responded to questions put by the Prosecution in relation to this statement. Therefore, we believe that this statement cannot be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, which statement are you referring to now, the old one or the new one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number one, I am talking about the old statement given in November 1993. And with your leave, I'm going to speak about this statement, when you ask me about that, and I'm going to be opposed to that, too, quite simply because in this statement that was given to an investigator two months ago, it says: "I stand by the statement I gave in November 1993."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you earlier said the statement of a person not done for the purposes of this court. Now, wouldn't that widen the options for admission if it is not taken for the purposes of proceedings before this court?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. But it's for the Prosecution to say, and not in this way as its been proposed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both documents will be MFI'd. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30758 receives number P6585. And document 30759 receives number P6586, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6585 and P6586 are marked for identification. We take a break but not until after the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've concluded my examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles. Just one little question. You referred to a SRNA interview, et cetera. Is there -- is that in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: It is not. It's referred to by Mr. Zulic. We do not have a copy of that SRNA interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Any further questions, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court document 65 ter 1D02275.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Andan, during the cross-examination by the Prosecutor, you were asked quite a few things about Brcko. This is what I'm asking you now. To the best of your recollection, in July 1992, after you left Brcko, this paramilitary formation, the Red Berets, was it placed under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please take a look at this together, paragraph 3 from the bottom of this report of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the next page in English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this dispatch that you're sending to the Ministry of the Interior on the 24th of July, 1992, among other things, you say: "Through our operative activities, we learned that the members of the Red Berets are still not subordinated to the military organs (twenty of them), and the Brcko garrison of the Serbian army gave them the dead-line to do so by 1800 hours." This is my question for you: Do you remember whether at any point in time these 20 or so members of the Red Berets joined the regular ranks of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice the unit of the police from Bijeljina intervened in Brcko. The first time we eliminated or we thought that we had eliminated the Red Berets. We went on other missions and they rose again, and the situation of chaos, if I can call it that, prevailed in Brcko once again. We intervened a second time and then there was an armed rebellion of the Red Berets because we had arrested most of their members and some of them became renegades. They even took some heavy weaponry with them and they went to Ugljevik. At that moment, I heard via radio communication that they had kidnapped Major Sehovac and they asked me to have their members released or they would kill Sehovac. I gave them a laconic answer: Kill him. If the Serb army has anything, it has plenty of officers. They didn't kill Sehovac. They handed over all the weapons. We made a list. They all hailed from Serbia, and at the Raca border crossing we gave them all to the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your experience in view of all the work you did in the police and the Army Republika Srpska, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, did they have the sincere intention of doing away with all of these paramilitary formations throughout Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My explicit answer is: Yes. This was an ongoing topic on the agenda of all meetings that I attended, that they should be disarmed, that they should be sent back to Serbia or other places that they had come from outside Bosnia-Herzegovina. At one point in time, it was more of a problem than the front line itself. However, in order to carry this through, a different kind of support was needed as well. You know how we faired in Bijeljina. This political support was not always on the side of those who wanted to settle scores with such criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am waiting for the interpretation. Please don't hold that against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court P501.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this document to be called up, Mr. Andan -- well, now you can see it in front of you. This is a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. The date is the 28th of July, 1992, and it is entitled: "Disarmament of Paramilitary Formations, Order -"

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like us to take a look at page 3 in the B/C/S version, or rather, the last page in the English version. I'm sorry, not this page but the previous page in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Signed General Ratko Mladic, commander of the Main Staff. Paragraph 2 of this order states as follows: [As read] "Individuals and groups which had carried out crimes, looting and other types of criminal acts are not to be included into units ... such persons are to be disarmed, arrested, and criminal proceedings are to be initiated against them in the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina army courts regardless of their citizenship." Paragraph 5 says, this is General Mladic's order: "I forbid all paramilitary formations, groups, and individuals in the territory of the SRBiH. In the future, criminal proceedings should be conducted against commanders, relevant military and territorial organs, and authorities who allow paramilitary organisation and evasion of recruitment and conscription in accordance with the SRBiH Law on the Army." In view of this document, this order of General Mladic's, your contacts with General Mladic, this is my question for you: Would this document precisely reflect the positions of General Mladic in terms of how paramilitary formations should be dealt with throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully. I know of several examples from my own practice. General Mladic issued an order if Arkan and his men moved towards the Drina that they should be arrested and that they should not be allowed to enter Republika Srpska at any cost. At one moment I heard him say, "If necessary, even use force and fire-arms when Arkan is in question."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again can we take a look at one of the documents used by the Prosecution, P6583.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a criminal report that has to do with the Yellow Wasps. We'll look at it together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 3 of this document in B/C/S, and I think that it's the same page in English. Yes. And it says here -- Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to the first paragraph in English version. In B/C/S can we please have the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, page 3. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not receive English translation. Could you please restart reading, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So this is a document that says the following and, Mr. Witness, could we please take a look at this together. Because of the suspicion that the following persons in a certain period in Karakaj from the 28th of June until the 29th of July, 1992, in Karakaj --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, now the English text starts on this page that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As for Zvornik, the group did not belong to the armed forces of the Serbian Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina," and then that is continued. After all these years and after all the testimony that you provided, do you still stand by the following: That these paramilitary formations, at the time when they were being arrested and at the time when they were doing what they were doing, did not belong to the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I absolutely stand by that, that they did not belong to the VRS. Those who were expelled and who returned were returned by certain political personages from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While we are still on this page where it says that you are charging them with the following, the commission of the crime of aggravated robbery, Article 151, paragraph 1 of the criminal code of the then-Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this is what I'm asking you now. If you remember. Do you remember that the minimum sentence is five years and the maximum sentence is 20 years in prison for that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to the old ZKP, it is 5 to 20 years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the law that was in force then, is that the most serious? Is that the highest sentence that can be imposed, 20 years in prison?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, could we please have the first page of this document. And I would like to conclude on that note.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This criminal report, according to this document, was first sent to the public prosecutor in Zvornik. Bijeljina was crossed out and then Zvornik was put there. Do you know that at that time there was a military prosecutor's office and a civilian prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what's the reason -- yes, I will slow down. I am sorry about this. The reason why this is being sent to the civilian prosecutor's office, is it because the status of these persons was that of civilians not military personnel? Is that your view?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if they were military personnel, we would have filed this with the military prosecutor's office. However, they were paramilitaries, they were therefore civilians, and we actually filed this criminal report with the civilian prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that the district court in Sabac in 1993 started criminal proceedings against Dusko Vuckovic, nicknamed Repic, because of the war crime of persecution of the civilian population, Article 142 of the criminal code of the former SFRY?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sent all the relevant documents to the MUP of Serbia because they were investigating the case of Repic then, and I know that Repic was sentenced to prison. I cannot remember what year that was and what the actual prison sentence was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I hope that we can stipulate. I hope that the Prosecution agrees. His prison sentence is a document that -- is stated in a document that we received from the OTP, and let me just say that the Defence states that he was found guilty and sentenced to ten years imprisonment and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. One second, please. Witness, you said that you didn't know when he was sentenced. Is it that you do not know the exact year or don't you know approximately when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't give you the exact year. But I know that he was sentenced and that he served his sentence. I've already told you that while we were in Bijeljina, we were requested to submit the relevant documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it briefly after he had committed those crimes that there was a prosecution and a sentence? Or was it long after that or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that question. I believe that a year or two or perhaps even three years lapsed before his trial was over, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not asking about how much time the trial took. I was asking when approximately that judgement was rendered, whether you have any recollection as even to approximately the period when that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, but I believe that the war was still on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means before December 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, if I knew I would tell you immediately. I know that he was sentenced but I don't know when that happened. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the parties assist me approximately about the year so that it can be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe 65 ter 30778 may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I'm usually not looking at 65 ter documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- unless they have been admitted into evidence. That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I believe that's the document Mr. Stojanovic was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So you apparently agree on the judgement. Could you tell me, then, what date appears on that judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If I'm reading this correctly, Your Honour, it appears that it would be July 8th of 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: July 8th, 1996. Thank you. Then, Mr. Stojanovic, anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just one more document and one more question. I would like to call up 65 ter, which also probably has a P number but I don't know it, 01925 is its 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, this is Exhibit P6579.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this document is what you already saw during the cross-examination. Let me first ask you a couple questions and then I will draw your attention to certain parts of this document. When it comes to the 1st Bijeljina Light Infantry Brigade, also known as the Panther Brigade, after having joined the VRS in November, as you said it yourself, and that was in 1992, was it one of the better organised and better equipped units in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that that unit, when it was engaged as a unit of the VRS, participated in any kind of crime?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear any such thing nor was there any police evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can I draw your attention to the document. In the preamble --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said one document, one question. I do understand that after the two questions you've put already on this document that you're now entering a new series of questions or?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. There have been a few questions, but I still need just one more document and this is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please conclude within a reasonable number of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the preamble of this document, it says that the commendation concerns the achievements in combat and the successful breakup of the offensive of the 5th Corps of the Muslim army. And it says the Combat Group Mauzer from the 1st Light Infantry Brigade in Bijeljina. When you read this document, would you draw an inference that the entire brigade was commended or just one part of that brigade known as Panther?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only a combat group was commended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then I will finish with the next question. You've had an occasion to be a guest on TV in Federal Sarajevo after the war. On that occasion, did the viewers called in? Were there any questions about the situations that you are testifying about today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was last year. I appeared on Alfa Television at their invitation. I arrived in Sarajevo. And I didn't know that it was a live show where the anchor and I were talking and viewers called in. There were questions from viewers about the group of Muslim members of the BiH army who surrendered in Bjelasnica and with whom I had immediate contact after that. I sent them to the Foca prison. From there they were exchanged, they went to Sarajevo, and after the war, a few of them contacted me and thanked me personally for my conduct towards them. And I have to say that there were no ugly questions from any of the viewers in that show. Before I testified here, I had to fill out a questionnaire for The Hague Tribunal where I mentioned my appearance on TV and I mentioned when that was staged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Adnan, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the questions in re-examination triggered any need for further questions? If not --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, is there any document you may have used which you wish to tender but have not tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Especially 1D2275?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. It's just one document that has not been admitted. And if I'm not mistaken, the 65 ter number is 1D2275. The other documents have already been admitted into evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2275 receives number D513, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. This, then, Mr. Andan, concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and you had to stay here for a couple of days, although the weather was not as bad as it often is. I'd like to thank you again for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would it be a common practice in this court for me to ask you something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may ask me something, but if it is about greeting of the accused, which is a question which is not -- okay, then please ask me whatever you want to ask --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's a professional question. In my police practice over the number of years, I've had a lot of investigative activities and interviews and we were always forbidden to put leading questions. I don't know whether this is the practice of this Court as well. However, during the cross-examination of the Prosecutor, I've had several leading questions which I don't think is in compliance with court practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, it is. In the common law tradition leading questions are usually admissible but in cross-examination only. So you noticed it right, that most of the leading questions were put to you in cross-examination which is acceptable in that system. Quite willing always perhaps at other moments to discuss legal matters but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I think I should give you a brief answer. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please don't hold it against us. The two of us come from the same legal system, hence our questions, dilemmas, and prejudices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness? No protective measures, the next witness being Mr. Guzina. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may Mr. Traldi and I be excused and leave you in capable other hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you mean the hands of Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, Mr. Guzina, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated. Mr. Guzina, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name for the record, but slowly.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Svetozar Guzina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you provided a statement to the Mladic Defence team about the war events?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 65 ter 1D01620.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you can see a page with your personal details and a signature. My question is whether these are your personal details and whether this signature is your signature?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Yes, this is information about me. This is my signature and the date is 15 May 2014. That's when I signed the document in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we go to the last page of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The document in front of you contains a witness confirmation, according to which you have provided the statement voluntarily, fully aware that it could be used before this Tribunal. Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today as are contained in your statement after having made a solemn declaration before this Court, would you still adhere to your entire statement?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Yes, I would adhere to my entire statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender the witness statement into evidence. The 65 ter number is 1D01620.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you submitted two versions of the statement, one confidential, the other publicly with some redactions. Which is which?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. I would kindly draw your attention to paragraph 8 in the witness statement and one of the footnotes says that the reason why we did that was the witness's request to -- not to broadcast the name mentioned in here for the reasons stated in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's turn into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Document 1D1620 is marked for identification under number D515 and under seal -- 514, I misspoke. 514, under seal, MFI'd. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please admit as associated exhibits the following documents. According to 65 ter they are 1D02123.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2123 receives number D515, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D515 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I would like to tender document 65 ter 1D02 -- actually, 1D02124.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2124 receives number D516, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D516 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I would like to tender 65 ter 1D02125.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2125 receives number D517, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Last one, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And finally, 1D02122.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2122 receives number D518, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D518 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, I would now like to read out a summary of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have not received a copy in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Svetozar Guzina, until the war broke out, lived as a restaurant owner in Sokolovic Kolonija. He was an eye-witness, an active participant in interethnic conflicts and armed incidents in his neighbourhood. He speaks about specific personal knowledge concerning the arming of the Muslims as early as spring 1991 until the war broke out. After he was forced to leave his home, he came to Ilidza and joined the Army of Republika Srpska. He became commander of the 5th Battalion and, after the reorganisation, the commander of the 1st Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade. He held that duty until the end of the war. The area of responsibility of his battalion was the area of Nedzarici. Throughout the period of the war, his order [as interpreted] had strict orders from the superior command that they should not fire at civilians. He personally obeyed that order and carried it through in his orders to his subordinates. He does not know of a single incident when civilians or civilian targets were targeted intentionally. He speaks about his experience when he had the positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the other side of the front line, and they were a legitimate military objective. He says that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, when fighting against his battalion, used vehicles on which mortars or machine-guns were mounted. Also, he will testify about his view of F9 and he says that it is an incomprehensible war situation; namely, that a civilian person at the time of fighting is moving in front of positions on the front line on the other side of the street, claiming that there were no sniper positions at that location. Finally, he testifies about humanitarian convoys and civilians moving through the area of responsibility of his battalion, and he says that he had orders from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to allow unhindered movement of convoys of humanitarian aid. Maybe I should start my questions after a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could do that. Then we take a break first, a break of 20 minutes. Witness, we'd like to see you back at 20 minutes to 2.00. And most likely cross-examination will then start at -- for the last 15 minutes, Mr. Stojanovic, I take it. The witness may follow the usher. We resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for not letting you know sooner, but just to make you aware that this witness received an admonishment pursuant to Rule 90(E) in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we discussed this thoroughly and we leave it -- not knowing what questions will be put to the witnesses, we leave it in the hands of the calling party whether or not they consider it wise to give a 90(E) warning. In most of the cases, as a matter of fact, there was no reason to believe that questions came even close to what could create a 90(E) situation. Therefore, we -- if Mr. Stojanovic would further encourage the Chamber to give a 90(E) warning, we would do it, but not at this moment. Further, D514 is admitted into evidence. It is the unredacted version of the statement. Now, the redacted version -- it's admitted under seal. The redacted version is already public as an attachment to the 92 ter motion. And since it's only a minor redaction, the public will not -- will have an opportunity to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, when I -- I was unclear. I started a sentence and didn't finish it. The unredacted version of the statement is admitted under seal and is D514. The redacted version was an attachment to the 92 ter motion and is available to the public. Then please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to call up 1D517, D517 that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'll ask you to look at the map. This is a map of Sarajevo, of course. Could you please help me and mark some of the places that we might find interesting. In paragraph 38 of your statement, you mention the old pensioners' home as the highest or tallest building in Nedzarici and that's where UNPROFOR troops were billeted and where their observation posts were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to provide the witness with a pen so that the witness may mark the facility where UNPROFOR had its observation post.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do I erase what I just marked because my marking should be a bit more to the left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This would be the place, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now you have just made a blue circle. Can you put the word "UNPROFOR" or just the two letters, UN, next to that circle?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to your recollection, how far was that facility from the institute for the blind children, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Some 200 to 250 metres. Or perhaps even less than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, in June 1994, when it comes to that facility, was there an observation post there also, an UNPROFOR observation post?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Yes. UNPROFOR took that building in late 1993 or early 1994. It was at the Serbian request because Muslim forces always provoked us and lied about fire being opened from our positions. With the consent of the brigade commander and the corps commander, we invited UNPROFOR to take up that facility to be able to observe the entire situation and to become aware of the lies uttered by the Muslims. And those lies were told all the time before they installed themselves on the roof of the old pensioners' home.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far was the old pensioners' home from the front line?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: If you look at the map, you will see that it is on the very front line because our positions were on the left-hand side of that street which ran through Nedzarici at the time. Effectively some 50 metres at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this part of the defence sector of your battalion, what was the distance between the positions of the BiH Army and the features that they occupied and your positions?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: The positions of the 1st Battalion in this area were on one side of the street, whereas the Muslim forces were on the other side of that same street. We were in the houses on one side of the street, which was our side, whether the -- the Muslim troops were in the buildings that were some 10-storeys high in the neighbourhood known as Dobrinja V. Those were very difficult positions. And I can say that the most difficult positions during the war were those in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you lived in Sarajevo before the war, when it comes to Alipasino Polje, Svrakino Selo, where was the police station before the war and during the war?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: I was in that police station on several occasions. My neighbour, Cedo Fabijancic [phoen] worked there. It would be across the street from the geodezik institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you make a mark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first of all slow down and make a break between question and answer, and answer and question, otherwise your words will be lost. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The witness marked or made a rather large circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to put letters PS next to that circle.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The letters will stand for the police station. Thank you. And while we have this exhibit on the screen, could you please tell me who was it who held the positions immediately behind your battalion, behind the airport runway?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Muslim forces, in Butmir neighbourhood. According to intelligence, that battalion faced my positions; i.e., the positions of the 1st Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During those war years, did you suffer from infantry and artillery fire opened from those positions of the BiH Army? Were you targeted from there?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Yes, from the very first day of the war we were targeted from Butmir across the airport runway. It was both artillery and infantry fire. We know that the artillery of that battalion in Butmir was in the institute. They constantly shelled our positions, the positions of my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will slow down while I wait for the interpretation. And now I will ask you to again take the pen and make a circle around the institute from which you were targeted.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And also draw arrows towards your positions --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: -- that were targeted from that sector.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now could you put letters AV, standing for the direction of the artillery fire you were exposed to, above the three arrows that you draw.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now, Your Honours, I would like to tender the marked map into the evidence of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document D517, as marked by the witness, receives number D519, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And is admitted into evidence. However, Mr. Stojanovic, if I look at the basis of this map, 517, as we started with, markings by the witness are -- I see here and there a -- not really a hand-made marking but apparently something. So I'm not questioning at this moment this one but rather 517. What exactly is found there? The witness said something about it, but whether these are clear markings is still to be seen. Perhaps you could later inform us about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'd like to draw your attention to a paragraph. Please bear with me. I'm looking for the relevant paragraph in the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I found it where it is when he said he marked certain positions. But whether an oval is the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as a square and a -- I do not know exactly. For the -- some of the features it's even unclear what building it is. I mean, for the Oslobodjenje and the students' home it seems to be pretty clear. But, for example, what is the case with the feature to the left of the Oslobodjenje building is -- what exactly is to be found in Stupsko Brdo is pretty unclear. I leave it to you perhaps to [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, while we still have the map in front of us, could you please tell the Chamber about the facility left to the Oslobodjenje building? It is marked with a rectangle. What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat and come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer and speak a bit closer into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next to the Oslobodjenje building, there was a new old pensioners' home. It was a multi-coloured building and we called it a parrot or a parrot building, papagajka [phoen], I believe that that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the position from which you were exposed by BiH Army fire?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Yes, continuously from day one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can you tell me about the rectangular facility somewhat below from the parrot building in the area of Stupsko Brdo?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Are we talking about the school of theology?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, apparently we're not because the theological faculty is a little bit further down and circled with an oval. I'm talking about the rectangular where the letters BR from Stupsko Brdo are found within that rectangular.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were Muslim positions, so this could be the so-called Betonara [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would that be the position from which you were exposed to BiH Army units' fire throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now as to the facilities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I read in the statement: "I have used red rectangles to mark the dominant features under Muslim control facing our zone." And -- yes, but I would like to know the specific one I referred to, that is, the rectangle where the letters BR are found within that rectangle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now I understand much better. The positions marked with rectangles were Muslim positions which we targeted throughout the war in response to their constant fire from the students' residential home, the furniture building -- factory building and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now what is then the position? Could you describe that? Was that the factory building, was it the -- the rectangle where we find the letters BR from Brdo within the rectangle, what kind of facility was that? What -- the position was housed in what or next to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a concrete building, a three-storey building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was not the concrete factory. It was not the Betonirka, but it was just a concrete building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, to the right of that there is an oval, next to where you marked AV. What does this oval exactly refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The oval shape represents the barracks in Nedzarici. It was under the control of Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, to say that it's very, very clear in paragraph 38 is another matter. But let's move on. This one was tendered, I think? I think it's admitted already. Madam Registrar? Then let's move on, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. And now I would like to call up 65 ter 11152.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement you described orders by the superior command with regard to the transport of humanitarian aid. I'm asking you this: When it comes to the defence sector of your battalion, were there any routes taken up by humanitarian convoys in order to reach Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Yes. We constantly let convoys through into the city of Sarajevo across our lines of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a standing order by the Main Staff throughout the war to comply with the procedure and to allow an unhindered passage of humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Yes, there was a procedure in place and throughout the war we allowed convoys through the Nedzarici check-point to go to Sarajevo. However, they had to comply with the procedure and they had to be announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the document that you see before you at the moment, it says -- and the document was issued by the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps on the 15th of May, 1993, it is titled: "An order for unhindered passage of humanitarian convoys." In the preamble, it says: "On the basis of directive by the Presidency of Republika Srpska, in order to comply with the cease-fire I order," and then what follows is the body of the text, where it says: "... ensure undisturbed passing and protection of the delivery, equipment, and personnel that is to help the civilian population of the opposing side." Under 2, it says that there is a ban on abuse. Under 3, full compliance with Geneva Conventions. And under 4, which is not marked with number 4 but it is the last paragraph, where it says that it should be ensured that all units and complete personnel of the SRK army get familiarised with this and respect this order. My question is this: Do you remember whether you had an occasion to see an order of this kind imposing on all the units of the SRK this type of conduct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: I am familiar with this order. This was implemented. Every single soldier was familiar with this order. Convoys were allowed to go through our check-points without any problems, save for perhaps one or two that were not duly announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also witness situations when convoys contained things that were not announced, some of which were military equipment and similar things?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of the war, when I was an operative in the Ilidza Brigade, a convoy that was en route from Ilidza to Butmir was stopped near the health institute and it was quite by incident that it was noted that there were some crates below the containers. When we lifted the containers, we found a lot of weapons which were carefully hidden between the containers en route to Butmir. Obviously, we seized all that, and after that, we became suspicious of UNPROFOR and all of their ensuing convoys. That's why we were very careful and we checked carefully the contents of those convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your personal relationship like with representatives of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: Well, this is what I can say. It was correct, especially with the liaison officers who liaised with me every day. On orders from the Main Staff and the corps, my duty was to talk to the liaison officer from UNPROFOR whenever necessary, so we had constant contact. I can actually take this opportunity to commend UNPROFOR. They did help me a great deal in one particular situation, because they let me know that the Muslim forces were digging two tunnels towards my positions. The second one was at Stupsko Brdo towards my positions near the barracks.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the first one the interpreter did not hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This really surprised me, this report that I received from them, very much so, because it came from the military observer from Jordan. But the man, probably when he saw what the situation was and when he saw how difficult the situation of my battalion was and how hard it was for me too, he informed me that the Muslims are building a tunnel, that they are digging a tunnel, that I should be careful. And as for this one tunnel at Stupsko Brdo, they actually crossed my lines, they killed two of my men and wounded some, and fighting for that position went on for an entire day. Only when a tank and APC were brought in I managed to resolve that position and to regain my position. It was in Serb hands again. Whereas the second tunnel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, I don't think, as a matter of fact, that the tunnels were the subject of questioning. You delved in that area. Next question, Mr. Stojanovic. You've used your time, by the way, but could you see whether there is one last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not receive English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we now hear you. Could you please restart your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That will be my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, during those four years of the war, how many members of your battalion were killed and how many were wounded?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA
utterances.text: In the 1st Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade, 167 soldiers were killed. About 400, and perhaps even a bit more, were wounded either once or a few times. I myself was wounded four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions of you. And now it is the Prosecutor who will be putting his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's still to be seen. I don't know whether it makes sense, Mr. Jeremy, to start. I would have one or two questions for the witness which I perhaps could put and then you will be cross-examined tomorrow. Witness, you were just shown an order consisting of three parts about the passage of humanitarian goods and the third one was about the Geneva Conventions. And you said every soldier was familiar with this order and it was implemented. Was every soldier also familiar with the third paragraph which is about the Geneva Conventions, were they aware of the contents of these conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that everyone was aware. At the very outset, at the very beginning of the war, there was this flyer that had come from the Presidency of the Republika Srpska, the President, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and that was what was written; namely, that the Geneva Conventions should be respected, and if people were taken prisoner, that the rights of prisoners, POWs, should be observed, and that civilians should not be fired at. So all soldiers of Republika Srpska knew that, how they were supposed to behave at any given point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you were in a command position, did you have thorough knowledge of these conventions and -- beyond what you just told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, roughly put. I mean, I was aware, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because if you say that you were instructed that prisoners of war should be -- the rights of prisoners of war should be observed, at least what you would need to know is what the rights of prisoners of war are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to give him water, to give him food, to protect him from further suffering. If he is wounded to take him to the hospital, to hand him over to further organs for their processing. That was our task and that is what we did. I have two cases that I can tell you about. Muslim children from Butmir crossed over to my position and they were safely returned, four of them. Also, there was this Muslim soldier, I know his name and surname, Cigic Alija, he was a neighbour of mine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you. Muslim children were treated in accordance with rules on prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I told you what happened in my situation and then you will decide whether this was right or not. These Muslim children were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm more puzzled by your understanding of what a prisoner of war is, because I've not heard ever of children being treated as prisoners of war under the regulations. It's -- at least it raises some doubt as to your knowledge of what a prisoner of war is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously we haven't understood each other. I am just giving you an example, something that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But an example --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An example of what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But my questions were about the rights of prisoners of war, and if you give as an example on how you treat a child, then this may raise some doubts as to your understanding of what a prisoner of war is. Could I ask you, could you tell me briefly because in paragraph 3 a distinction is made between the convention of the law on customs of war -- of a land war, 1907, and the Geneva Conventions. Could you briefly explain to me where is approximately the difference between this 1907 convention on the law of land and the Geneva Conventions of 1949? Could you tell me approximately where is to be found under one -- in one and what is to be found in the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, I am not an officer who attended officers school. I am a man who is in the catering business, who owned a restaurant of his own, who completed a school for catering and tourism, and I didn't really deal with such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing that I'm exploring is what it means if one says this was fully implied if you do not know exactly what it is about. Now, I'm not blaming you, I'm just asking you whether you could give me what is to be found under one and what is to be found in the other. Apparently, you can't tell me, and there may be good reasons for that, I was not asking yet about the reasons. So do I understand your answer to be that you could not tell us what approximately is found in the one and what is approximately found in the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Could -- I would like to -- we will adjourn for the day and I would like to ask you to come back tomorrow morning at 9.30. And meanwhile, I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony you have given today or whether it's testimony still to be given tomorrow. And then we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 11th of June, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 11th day of June, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.19 p.m.,
